text: Many say it’s best to save face and work things out privately, but I’d disagree. If you don’t have friends who can help with the conflict, then you’re really stuck (and you might wanna find some new friends). But do it fairly, with the goal of helping the conflict, not just getting approval for your own interpretation. Both people should get a chance to speak, and good friends should hear both sides before validating either.
reader: someone reading an essay on romance for advice they can use in their own dating and relationships

sentences.s: Many say it’s best to save face and work things out privately, but I’d disagree.
sentences.payoff: they learn the author advises against handling conflict privately to save face, so they consider telling someone.
sentences.follows: the heading is about conflict that stays hidden, and this takes the position against keeping it private.
sentences.link: none: opens the section on the author's position

sentences.payoff: they learn that having no friend to turn to is the real problem and worth fixing.

sentences.s: But do it fairly, with the goal of helping the conflict, not just getting approval for your own interpretation.
sentences.payoff: they learn the condition for bringing a friend in: aim at helping the conflict, not at winning approval.
sentences.follows: it turns from having friends (S2) to how to use them.

sentences.s: Both people should get a chance to speak, and good friends should hear both sides before validating either.
sentences.payoff: they know to tell the friend the other side and expect a friend who hears both before judging.
sentences.follows: it says what 'fairly' means in S3.
sentences.link: Both people should get a chance

placement: It follows the heading about gaslighting in the dark as the remedy, taking conflicts out of privacy, so the reader has something to do about their own interpretation being the only one.

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")?
